newsitem.title: USA: November retail sales drop, prices muted.
newsitem.headline: November retail sales drop, prices muted.

text.p: Retail sales posted a surprising drop during November in the approach to the Christmas shopping season, the government said on Thursday, while prices that consumers paid for everything from food to clothing rose modestly.
Dragged down by a plunge in new-car sales, overall retail sales fell 0.4 percent in November to a seasonally adjusted $206.1 billion despite a predicted increase.

It was the first sales decline since a 0.1 percent fall in August and followed a 0.3 percent October rise, the Commerce Department said. Excluding automobiles, November sales were up a slim 0.3 percent after a 0.4 percent October gain.

Separately, the Labour Department said its Consumer Price Index registered a 0.3 percent rise last month, the same as in October, but rose only 0.2 percent once volatile food and energy costs were stripped out.

Analysts said the reports portrayed an economy expanding slowly but steadily, still free of the threat of stronger inflation and highly unlikely to force Federal Reserve policy-makers to boost interest rates next week as a restraint on growth.

"Basically, we continue to have an economy growing in line with trend growth, not too fast and not too slow, consistent with inflation containment," said Robert Dederick, an economic consultant to Northern Trust Co. in Chicago.

Another report on Thursday from the Labour Department showed a sharp plunge in new claims for unemployment benefits last week -- to 317,000 from 330,000 in the prior week -- underlining tight labour markets and plentiful jobs.

Strong job markets often bring demands for higher wages that can push up prices. But analysts said ample supplies of cheap consumer goods from countries like China and spending restraint by shoppers have kept a lid on prices in stores and factories.
"It's essentially an economy that is comfortably mired in prosperity," observed Dederick. "It is just what a central banker dreams about."

The Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets for a final time this year on Tuesday to plot interest-rate strategy. It has not changed rates since last January and is not expected to do so next week.
Exceptionally weak auto-dealer sales were the key reason for the falloff in November retail sales, though there were ample other indications of consumer tight-fistedness.
Auto-dealer sales plummeted 2.6 percent to $49.5 billion -- the biggest drop since a 3.5 percent fall in April, when they were down 3.5 percent. Auto sales had risen a slight 0.1 percent in October.

New cars account for about one-fifth of total retail sales, so swings in demand strongly affect the overall monthly figures. Excluding cars, retail sales were up 0.3 percent last month after gaining 0.4 percent in October.
The retail industry shook off slow November sales and predicted a bounceback in December as Christmas approaches.
The Thanksgiving Day holiday was later this year than last, so the traditional post-Thanksgiving holiday sales season got a late start.

Economist Rosalind Wells of the National Retail Federation, which represents more than 1 million store-owners, said surveys showed sales on the upswing in the abbreviated four-week Christmas season, when retailers do most of their business.
"Economic indicators remain positive and retailers are reporting brisk sales in December," Wells said, adding, "All this points to solid gains and profits for Holiday 1996."

Sales of all types of durable goods, from cars to hardware and building materials, fell 1.1 percent in November to $83.5 billion after rising 0.3 percent in October. Sales of non-durable goods like food and clothing edged up 0.1 percent to $122.5 billion following a 0.4 percent October increase.

Sales by general merchandise stores fell 0.6 percent to $25.8 billion after a 0.4 percent gain in October. At apparel stores, sales of clothing dropped 0.9 percent to $9.4 billion after falling 0.6 percent in October.

The report on consumer price rises was widely seen as reassuring evidence that inflation was dormant at the consumer level as well as among producers. On Wednesday, the Labour Department said producer prices rose 0.4 percent in November but were up just a mild 0.1 percent excluding energy costs.
"The overall impression the report leaves us with is inflation remains as well-behaved as we all thought it was," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets.
